source_text:
Audio poetas quoque unum patrem diuum atque hominum praedicantes, et talem esse mortalium mentem qualem parens omnium diem induxerit. quid Mantuanus Maro ?
nonne apertius, proximius, uerius principio ait caelum ac terras et cetera mundi membra spiritus intus alit et infusa mens agitat, inde hominum pecudumque genus et quicquid aliud animalium? idem alio loco mentem istam et spiritum deum nominat. haec enim uerba sunt: deum namque ire per omnes terrasque tractusque maris caelumque profundum, unde homines et pecudes, unde imber et ignes.
quid aliud et a nobis Deus quam mens et ratio et spiritus praedicatur? recenseamus, si placet, disciplinam philosophorum: deprehendes eos, etsi sermonibus uariis, ipsis tamen rebus in hanc unam coire et conspirare sententiam.
omitto illos rudes et ueteres, qui de suis dictis sapientes esse meruerunt. sit Thales Milesius omnium primus, qui primus omnium de caelestibus disputauit. is autem Milesius Thales rerum initium aquam dixit, deum autem eam mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formauerit: [eo altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ut ab homine potuerit inueniri, a deo traditum] : uides philosophi principalis nobiscum penitus opinionem consonare.
Anaximenes deinceps et post ApolloniatesDiogenes aera deum statuunt infinitum et inmensum: horum quoque similis de diuinitate consensio est.
Anaiagorae uero descriptio et motus infinitae mentis deus dicitur, et Pythagorae deus est animus per uniuersam rerum naturam commeans et intentus, ex quo etiam animalium omnium uita capiatur.
Xenophanen notum est omne infinitum cum mente deum tradere, et Antisthenen populares deos multos, sed naturalem unum praecipuum, Speusippum uim [natn.ralem] animalem, qua omnia regantur, Deum nosse.
quid ? Democritus, quamuis atomorum primus inuentor, nonne plerumque naturam quae imagines fundat et intellegentiam deum loquitur? Straton quoque et ipse naturam? etiam Epicurus ille, qui deos aut otiosos fingit aut nullos, naturam tamen superponit.
Aristoteles uariat et adsignat tamen unam potestatem: nam interim mentem, mundum interim deum dicit, interim mundo deum praeficit. Heraclides Ponticus quoque deo diuinam mentem quamuis uarie adscribit.
Theophrastus etiam uariat, alias mundo, alias menti diuinae tribuens principatum. Zenon et Chrysippus et Cleanthes sunt et ipsi multiformes, sed ad unitatem prouidentiae omnes reuoluuntur. Cleanthes enim mentem, modo animum, modo aethera, plerumque rationem deum disseruit. Zenon, eiusdem magister, naturalem legem atque diuinam et aethera interim interdumque rationem uult omnium esse principium; idem interpretando Iunonem aera, Iouem caelum, Neptunum mare, ignem esse Vulcanum et ceteros similiter uulgi deos elementa esse monstrando publicum arguit grauiter et reuincit errorem.
eadem fere Chrysippus: uim diuinam, rationalem naturam et mundum interim et fatalem necessitatem deum credit Zenonemque interpretatione physiologica in Hesiodi, Homeri Orpheique carminibus imitatur.
Babylonio etiam Diogeni disciplina est exponendi et disserendi, louis partum et ortum Mineruae et hoc genus cetera rerum uocabula esse, non deorum.
nam Socraticus Xenophon formam dei ueri negat uideri posse et ideo quaeri non oportere, Ariston Stoicus conprehendi omnino non posse: uterque maiestatem Dei intellegendi desperatione senserunt.
Platoni apertior de deo et rebus ipsis et nominibus oratio est et quae tota esset caelestis, nisi persuasionis ciuilis nonnumquam admixtione sordesceret. Platoni itaque in Timaeo deus est ipso suo nomine mundi parens, artifex animae, caelestium terrenorumque fabricator, quem et inuenire difficile prae nimia et incredibili potestate, et cum inueneris, in publicum dicere inpossibile praefatur.
eadem fere sunt ista, quae nostra sunt: nam et Deum nouimus et parentem omnium dicimus et numquam publice nisi interrogati praedicamus.
thought_title: Philosophers agree on one divine mind
orientation: Octavius is speaking, arguing that even pagan poets and philosophers point to one divine mind or reason, which matches the Christian understanding of God.
pass_a_gloss: Listen also to the poets proclaiming one father of gods and of humans, and that the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all has brought in as the day. What of Mantuan Maro? Does he not more openly, more closely, more truly say at the beginning that a spirit within nourishes heaven and earth and the other members of the world, and an infused mind stirs them, and from there the race of humans and cattle and whatever else of animals? The same man in another place names that mind and spirit God. For these are the words: for God goes through all lands and tracts of sea and deep heaven, from where humans and cattle, from where rain and fires. What else is proclaimed by us than that God is mind and reason and spirit? Let us review, if you please, the teaching of the philosophers: you will discover that they, although with varied words, nevertheless in the things themselves come together and agree into this one opinion. I pass over those rude and ancient ones, who from their own sayings deserved to be called wise. Let Thales of Miletus be first of all, who first of all disputed about heavenly things. That Milesian Thales said that the beginning of things is water, but that God is that mind which formed all things from water: so much higher and more sublime is the reason of water and spirit than that it could have been found by a human, handed down by God: you see that the opinion of the chief philosopher agrees deeply with us. Anaximenes next, and after him Diogenes of Apollonia, establish that air is God, infinite and immense: of these too there is a similar agreement about divinity. But the description and motion of infinite mind is called God by Anaxagoras, and for Pythagoras God is a soul passing through and intent upon the whole nature of things, from which also the life of all animals is taken. It is known that Xenophanes hands down all that is infinite with mind as God, and that Antisthenes knows many popular gods but one natural one as chief, and that Speusippus knows God as a natural animal force by which all things are ruled. What? Democritus, although the first inventor of atoms, does he not often speak of nature which pours out images and intelligence as God? Strato too, does he not himself speak of nature? Even that Epicurus, who either imagines gods as idle or as none, nevertheless places nature above. Aristotle varies and yet assigns one power: for sometimes he calls it mind, sometimes the world God, sometimes he sets God over the world. Heraclides Ponticus also ascribes divine mind to God, although variously. Theophrastus also varies, sometimes assigning the chief place to the world, sometimes to divine mind. Zeno and Chrysippus and Cleanthes are themselves also multiform, but they all return to the unity of providence. For Cleanthes discussed God as mind, sometimes as soul, sometimes as aether, often as reason. Zeno, his teacher, wants natural and divine law and aether sometimes and at other times reason to be the beginning of all things; the same man, by interpreting Juno as air, Jupiter as heaven, Neptune as sea, Vulcan as fire, and by showing that the other gods of the common crowd are similarly elements, gravely argues against and refutes the public error. Chrysippus does almost the same: he believes that divine force, rational nature and the world sometimes and fatal necessity is God, and he imitates Zeno in the physiological interpretation in the poems of Hesiod, Homer and Orpheus. For Diogenes of Babylon too the discipline is of explaining and discussing, that the birth of Jupiter and the origin of Minerva and other things of this kind are names of things, not of gods. For the Socratic Xenophon denies that the form of the true God can be seen and therefore that it ought not to be sought, Aristo the Stoic that it cannot be grasped at all: both sensed the majesty of God through despair of understanding. Plato's speech about God is more open both in the things themselves and in the names, and it would be entirely heavenly, if it did not sometimes become soiled by the admixture of civic persuasion. For Plato in the Timaeus, God is by his own name the parent of the world, the artificer of the soul, the fabricator of heavenly and earthly things, whom he says beforehand is difficult to find because of his excessive and incredible power, and when you have found him, impossible to speak of in public. These things are almost the same as our things: for we both know God and call him parent of all, and we never proclaim him publicly except when asked.

choices.english: one father of gods and of humans
choices.why: Keeps the poetic phrase's parallelism and the singular 'one' that Octavius emphasizes.
rejected: a single father of gods and men

choices.why: Preserves the Vergilian word order and the interiority of 'intus'.
Uses the glossary terms for mens, ratio, spiritus to keep Octavius's triad exact.

choices.term: in hanc unam coire et conspirare sententiam
choices.english: come together and agree into this one opinion
choices.why: Renders both verbs literally to show the convergence Octavius claims.

choices.term: publicum arguit grauiter et reuincit errorem
choices.english: gravely argues against and refutes the public error
choices.why: Keeps the legal force of arguit and reuincit, which fits Minucius's lawyerly style.
rejected: severely convicts and disproves the common mistake

choices.english: would become soiled by the admixture of civic persuasion
choices.why: Literal rendering of sordesceret preserves the moral stain Octavius sees in Plato's concessions.
rejected: would be tainted by occasional political accommodation

pass_b_english: Listen also to the poets, who proclaim one father of gods and of humans, and say that the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all things has brought the day. What about Vergil of Mantua? Does he not say, more openly, more closely, more truly, at the beginning: 'A spirit within nourishes heaven and earth and the other members of the world, and an infused mind stirs them; from this comes the race of humans and beasts and whatever other living things there are'? Elsewhere he calls that mind and spirit God. These are his words: 'For God passes through all lands and the stretches of the sea and the deep sky; from him come humans and beasts, from him rain and fires.' What else do we proclaim God to be than mind and reason and spirit?

Let us review, if you please, the teaching of the philosophers: you will find that, although their words vary, they nevertheless come together and agree into this one opinion in the things themselves. I pass over those rough and ancient thinkers who earned the name of wise men from their sayings. Let Thales of Miletus be first of all, since he was the first of all to discuss heavenly matters. This Thales of Miletus said that the beginning of things was water, but that God was the mind which formed all things from water: [a later gloss adds: the account of water and spirit is too lofty and sublime for a human being to have found it; it was handed down by God]. You see that the opinion of the first philosopher agrees deeply with ours.

Anaximenes next, and after him Diogenes of Apollonia, establish air as God, infinite and immeasurable: their agreement about divinity is similar as well. Anaxagoras's description and motion of an infinite mind is called God, and Pythagoras's God is a soul passing through and intent upon the whole nature of things, from which the life of all living things is taken. It is well known that Xenophanes handed down that God is everything infinite with mind, and that Antisthenes knew many popular gods but one natural God as chief, and that Speusippus knew God as a natural living force by which all things are governed.

What of Democritus? Although he was the first inventor of atoms, does he not often speak of nature, which pours out images, and intelligence as God? Straton too—does he not also call nature God? Even that Epicurus, who imagines gods either idle or nonexistent, nevertheless places nature above them. Aristotle varies, yet he assigns one power: for sometimes he calls mind God, sometimes the world, sometimes he places God over the world. Heraclides of Pontus also ascribes a divine mind to God, though in varying ways.

Theophrastus also varies, at one time giving the chief place to the world, at another to the divine mind. Zeno and Chrysippus and Cleanthes are themselves also of many forms, but they all return to the unity of providence. Cleanthes discussed God as mind, sometimes as soul, sometimes as aether, and most often as reason. Zeno, his teacher, wants natural and divine law, and aether, and sometimes reason, to be the beginning of all things; by interpreting Juno as air, Jupiter as heaven, Neptune as sea, Vulcan as fire, and by showing that the other gods of the crowd are similarly elements, he gravely argues against and refutes the public error.

Chrysippus holds almost the same view: he believes God to be divine force, rational nature, sometimes the world, and sometimes fatal necessity, and he imitates Zeno in the physiological interpretation of the poems of Hesiod, Homer, and Orpheus. Diogenes of Babylon also has a method of explaining and arguing that the birth of Jupiter and the origin of Minerva and other things of this kind are names of things, not of gods. For Xenophon the Socratic denies that the form of the true God can be seen and therefore says he should not be sought; Aristo the Stoic says he cannot be comprehended at all: both of them perceived the majesty of God through the despair of understanding him.

Plato's speech about God is more open, both in the things themselves and in the names, and it would be entirely heavenly if it were not sometimes soiled by the admixture of civic persuasion. In the Timaeus, then, Plato says that God is by his very name the parent of the world, the artisan of the soul, the maker of heavenly and earthly things, and he says beforehand that it is difficult to find him because of his excessive and incredible power, and that when you have found him, it is impossible to speak of him in public. These things are almost the same as ours: for we know God and call him the parent of all things, and we never proclaim him publicly unless we are asked.

problems.quote: the mind of mortals is whatever kind of day the parent of all things has brought in
problems.source_quote: talem esse mortalium mentem qualem parens omnium diem induxerit
problems.why: diem induxerit means 'has brought in daylight/dawn', not 'has brought in day'; the sense is about illumination/enlightenment of mind by God, not temporal 'day'
problems.fix: the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all things has brought to light
problems.ruling: Latin says mind is as the day introduced by the parent, implying illumination; English renders as 'whatever kind of day' misrepresenting meaning

problems.quote: so much higher and more sublime is the reason of water and spirit than that it could have been discovered by a human being
problems.source_quote: eo altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ut ab homine potuerit inueniri, a deo traditum
problems.why: The bracketed text is a gloss/commentary, not Thales' words; 'ratio' here means 'account/explanation', not 'reason'; and 'a deo traditum' refers to the teaching being handed down by God, not the reason of water and spirit
problems.fix: [omit or bracket as gloss] the higher and more sublime account of water and spirit, than that it could be found by man, handed down by God
problems.ruling: Translation omits 'a deo traditum' (handed down by God) and misattributes gloss as Thales' words, altering meaning

edits.old: the mind of mortals is whatever kind of day the parent of all things has brought in
edits.new: the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all things has brought to light

edits.old: so much higher and more sublime is the reason of water and spirit than that it could have been discovered by a human being—it was handed down by God
edits.new: the account of water and spirit is higher and more sublime than that it could have been discovered by a human being—it was handed down by God

fixed: Corrected 'diem induxerit' to 'has brought to light' (illumination sense), matching 'talem esse mortalium mentem qualem parens omnium diem induxerit'.

Changed 'reason of water and spirit' to 'account of water and spirit' and removed 'so much' to reflect the bracketed gloss as commentary, per 'eo altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ut ab homine potuerit inueniri, a deo traditum'.

problems.quote: a mind infused through them stirs them
problems.source_quote: spiritus intus alit et infusa mens agitat
problems.why: 'intus alit' means 'nourishes within' not 'infused through them'; 'infusa mens' is 'infused mind' not 'mind infused through them'
problems.fix: a spirit within nourishes, and an infused mind stirs
problems.ruling: Misreads ‘spiritus intus alit’ and ‘infusa mens’ as ‘mind infused through them’

problems.quote: the account of water and spirit is higher and more sublime than that it could have been discovered by a human being
problems.source_quote: eo altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ut ab homine potuerit inueniri, a deo traditum
problems.why: Bracketed text in source is likely interpolation; but translated, 'eo...quam ut' means 'so much higher...than that,' and 'ratio' is 'account/reasoning' not 'the account'; 'a deo traditum' lacks verb
problems.fix: [omit bracketed interpolation or mark as such]
problems.ruling: Omits ‘a deo traditum’ and mis‑renders ‘eo…quam ut’, losing divine authority

problems.quote: everything infinite with mind is God
problems.source_quote: omne infinitum cum mente deum tradere
problems.why: 'tradere' means 'handed down/teaches' not 'is'; Xenophanes teaches God is 'all infinite with mind' or 'infinite mind'
problems.fix: Xenophanes handed down that God is all infinite mind
problems.ruling: Turns verb ‘tradere’ (teach) into copula ‘is’, changing meaning

problems.quote: and he says beforehand that it is difficult to find him
problems.source_quote: quem et inuenire difficile prae nimia et incredibili potestate, et cum inueneris, in publicum dicere inpossibile praefatur
problems.why: 'praefatur' governs both clauses; 'praefatur' means 'says beforehand/prefaces' but 'quem' is object of both 'inuenire' and 'dicere'; 'praefatur' takes accusative+infinitive
problems.fix: whom he prefaces is difficult to find because of his excessive and incredible power, and impossible to speak of in public when you have found him
problems.ruling: Omits second clause about impossibility of speaking of him publicly

edits.old: a mind infused through them stirs them
the account of water and spirit is higher and more sublime than that it could have been discovered by a human being—it was handed down by God.
edits.new: the account of water and spirit is so much higher and more sublime than that it could have been discovered by a human being—it was handed down by God.

edits.old: everything infinite with mind is God
edits.new: God is everything infinite with mind

edits.old: and he says beforehand that it is difficult to find him because of his excessive and incredible power, and that when you have found him, it is impossible to speak of him in public.
edits.new: and he says beforehand that it is difficult to find him because of his excessive and incredible power, and that when you have found him, it is impossible to speak of him in public.

fixed: Changed 'a mind infused through them stirs them' to 'an infused mind stirs them': source 'infusa mens agitat' has 'infusa' as adjective modifying 'mens', not 'infused through them'.

Added 'so much' to 'the account of water and spirit is higher and more sublime': source 'eo altior et sublimior...quam ut' means 'so much higher...than that'; the English omitted the correlative force of 'eo'.

Changed 'everything infinite with mind is God' to 'God is everything infinite with mind': source 'omne infinitum cum mente deum tradere' has 'deum' as the predicate accusative of 'tradere', so Xenophanes teaches that God is all that is infinite with mind, not that everything infinite is God.

Left the Plato sentence unchanged: the English 'and he says beforehand that it is difficult to find him...and that when you have found him, it is impossible to speak of him in public' correctly renders 'quem et inuenire difficile...et cum inueneris, in publicum dicere inpossibile praefatur'; 'praefatur' governs both clauses and the English already reflects this.

problems.quote: the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all things has brought to light
problems.source_quote: talem esse mortalium mentem qualem parens omnium diem induxerit
problems.why: diem = day, not 'brought to light'; should be 'as the parent of all has brought the day'
problems.fix: the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all things has brought the day
problems.ruling: Latin adds ‘diem’ (day) which English omits, altering the meaning

problems.quote: the account of water and spirit is so much higher and more sublime than that it could have been discovered by a human being
problems.source_quote: eo altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ut ab homine potuerit inueniri, a deo traditum
problems.why: Missing 'a deo traditum' (handed down by God) in main text; bracketed in source but part of transmitted text
problems.fix: the account of water and spirit is higher and more sublime than to have been found by man: it was handed down by God
problems.ruling: Phrase ‘a deo traditum’ (handed down by God) is omitted, losing a key attribution

edits.old: the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all things has brought to light
edits.new: the mind of mortals is such as the parent of all things has brought the day

edits.old: the account of water and spirit is so much higher and more sublime than that it could have been discovered by a human being—it was handed down by God.
edits.new: the account of water and spirit is higher and more sublime than to have been found by a human being: it was handed down by God.

fixed: Corrected 'brought to light' to 'brought the day' to match source 'diem induxerit'.
Restored the missing 'handed down by God' clause and adjusted the comparison to match source 'eo altior et sublimior aquae et spiritus ratio, quam ut ab homine potuerit inueniri, a deo traditum'.

fixed.quote: the account of water and spirit is higher and more sublime than to have been found by a human being: it was handed down by God
fixed.fix: [a later gloss adds: the account of water and spirit is too lofty and sublime for a human being to have found it; it was handed down by God]
fixed.note: The copy-text brackets this sentence as an interpolation, but the English presents it as Minucius's own words, and its wording is clumsy.
